column3: The immediate continuation says God will record the claimant's words and extend his punishment.
It joins possessed wealth, its eschatological consequence, and God's ultimate inheritance of all things.
It states the focus's final outcome directly: every person comes to God alone on the Day of Resurrection.
Zechariah's plea not to be left alone and his address to God as best heir form a meaningful inverse parallel.
Mary's withdrawal behind a veil does not clarify inheritance, the claim, or solitary return.
God's complete knowledge of speech supports the focus's accountability for what the claimant says.
People come to God individually, leaving behind their granted possessions and claimed intercessors.
This is the claimant's preceding boast that he will receive wealth and children, answered in the focus.
Its demand for proof against invented gods does not develop the claimant's wealth, inheritance, or return.
The inheritance of scripture by Israel is a distinct, positive form of succession rather than God's taking the claimant's possessions.
Jesus receiving scripture and prophethood does not clarify the focus's warning to the claimant.
It gives the surah's general statement that God inherits the earth and all upon it before their return to Him.
The hypocrites' speech is blameworthy, but its particular complaint does not illuminate the focus.
The immediate preceding question exposes the claimant's unsupported certainty about his future wealth and children.
The garden owners' reaction to their loss has no material link to the focus's claim or solitary return.
A balanced prayer for worldly and final good only broadly contrasts with the claimant's presumptuous worldly promise.
After destroying affluent towns, God remains their heir, closely supporting the reversal of temporary possession in the focus.
Turning away from signs does not specifically develop inheritance or arriving alone.
At fulfillment, forgotten deniers lose their invented claims and face the consequences of their past words.
It names the day people come to God, directly framing the arrival stated in the focus.
Its challenge to produce alleged partners gives a distant parallel to unsupported claims before judgment.
The transfer of Pharaoh's former possessions to Israel is a historical, human inheritance rather than the focus's divine taking.
The abundance of Paradise fruit does not clarify the claimant's loss of wealth and children.
The introduction to Moses's story has no relevant neighbour relation.
Solomon's inheritance from David provides a legitimate human succession that contrasts with the claimant's imagined security.
God makes the oppressed heirs, showing that inheritance and succession are assigned by God rather than secured by pretension.
The human question at the earth's upheaval has no specific relation to the focus.
The prohibition on a prophet claiming worship for himself only broadly cautions against unauthorized speech.
It establishes that everyone in heaven and earth comes to the Merciful as a servant, grounding the claimant's solitary return.
The promise that guidance will come offers only a broad future-arrival parallel.
Standing before God in pairs or alone meaningfully echoes the focus's emphasis on the individual.
God's empowerment of the oppressed contrasts broadly with the claimant's assumed future possession.
Calling believers heirs introduces a different, positive inheritance with little detail about the focus's warning.
The possibility of showing promised punishment to the Prophet does not clarify this claimant's fate.
The granting of Yahya to Zechariah is a positive family succession, unlike the claimant who comes without companions.
Its instruction to pardon until God's command comes has no direct relation to the focus.
God's transcendence over what people say supports the rejection of the claimant's presumptuous assertion.
Divine provision of worldly goods offers only a general counterpart to the claimant's hoped-for wealth and children.
Deniers defer faith until the punishment of former peoples or the punishment itself comes before them.
Yahya's compassion, purity, and piety do not illuminate the focus's warning.
God's provision of livestock and sons gives a concrete counterpart to the claimant's boast of wealth and children.
God gathers everyone together, supporting the focus's final return even though it does not specify solitude.
The reminder that God was not unjust does not clarify the focus.
The command to call to God and avoid association does not develop inheritance or solitary arrival.
God encompasses even concealed, unacceptable speech, supporting the focus's accounting for what is said.
The arrival of certainty closes the time for denial, parallel to the claimant's eventual unavoidable return.
Concern for vulnerable descendants and upright speech gives a sober ethical contrast to boasting of descendants.
Its legal duties of an heir concern family maintenance, only remotely related to divine inheritance in the focus.
God knows exactly what people say, providing a close accountability parallel to the focus's mention of speech.
Paradise inherited for deeds is a distinct positive inheritance, not the loss of claimed possessions.
Abraham's prayer to be among Paradise's heirs offers a positive eschatological inheritance parallel.
God gives life and death and is the ultimate heir, directly explaining why every temporary holder loses possession.
Inheriting Paradise is related only as a contrasting positive form of inheritance.
The ignorant repeat a demand in speech, but it does not address the focus's particular claim or outcome.
Their demand for a sign is another blameworthy saying, with only a distant relation to the focus.
The pursuit at sunrise has no material relation to the focus.
Those who ignored God's signs are themselves forgotten on the Day, a related warning of final reversal.
Turning from remembrance leads to distress and resurrection, framing the claimant's eventual return for judgment.
Human inheritance shares the vocabulary but does not clarify God's inheritance of the claimant's claim.
The challenged people demand punishment but the verse does not develop the focus's themes.
Denying the Day of Recompense broadly relates to the final accountability in the focus.
The extended columns of punishment do not clarify inheritance, speech, or solitary arrival.
God's absolute oneness provides a broad theological basis for exclusive divine ownership, but no direct neighbour link.
God created a man alone before granting wealth and sons, strongly paralleling the claimant's loss of such supports.
The inheritance distribution and kind speech concern social duty, not the focus's eschatological warning.
Moses receiving scripture does not develop the focus.
The condemned person's regret that he did not prepare for his true life closely parallels arriving alone after worldly wealth fails.
The demand that angels be brought has no specific relation to the focus.
God's effective command gives a general contrast to the claimant's unsupported saying, but not a direct link.
The transfer of a people’s former property to another people is only a historical echo of inheritance.
God's creative command is a distant contrast to the claimant's human speech.
The futile prayer of disbelievers after proof has come broadly anticipates their final helplessness.
Mary's question about having a child concerns miraculous creation, not the claimant's boast or loss.
Persistent turning from signs gives a general context for eventual judgment, without a direct focus relation.
Zechariah's prayer for an heir supplies the positive, faithful use of inheritance language within the same surah.
The dispute over being approached from the right does not clarify the focus.
The question about belief in resurrection has no specific inheritance or solitary-return relation.
Moses arriving at the fire does not clarify the claimant's arrival to God.
A false profession of faith is blameworthy speech but lacks the focus's themes of wealth, inheritance, and return.
Devouring inheritance exposes wrongful attachment to accumulated property, a useful worldly contrast to God's ultimate inheritance.
God grants Paradise as an inheritance to pious servants, the positive counterpart to the claimant's possessions reverting to God.
The truth came to the deniers while they lied, broadly reinforcing the focus's rejection of the claimant's assertion.
The request to identify the cow does not clarify the focus.
The appointed meeting with God is certainly coming, directly supporting the focus's statement that the claimant will come to Him.
Responses to a newly revealed surah concern another kind of speech and do not develop the focus's outcome.
At the approach to God, only a sound heart avails, strongly clarifying why worldly wealth and children cannot accompany the claimant.
The question about the cow's color has no relevant connection.
Mocking every messenger is a general form of rejection, but it does not explain the claimant's loss or solitude.
The prayer for worldly gain without a share in the Hereafter sharply contrasts with the focus's collapse of worldly expectations.
The news mocked by deniers will come to them as reality, paralleling the focus's promised consequence.
The decisive word offers only a broad connection to God's final judgment on human claims.
The command to seek refuge does not clarify the focus's inheritance or final arrival.
The believers' plea to avert Hell's punishment broadly parallels the punishment following the claimant's words.
The sudden coming of the Hour or punishment gives a close eschatological-arrival parallel.
Prayer for faithful descendants provides a positive family contrast but does not develop the focus directly.
God makes the oppressed inherit lands after destroying their oppressors, illustrating His reversal of temporary dominion.
Jacob's complaint to God and special knowledge do not materially clarify the focus.
Those held back plead that wealth and families occupied them while God exposes their spoken excuse and sole control over benefit and harm.
The command not to defraud people in their goods only generally concerns material responsibility.
When God's command comes, truth is decided and falsifiers lose, matching the focus's final negation of a false claim.
The same surah contrasts transient boasting with lasting righteous deeds, which are better in reward and final return.
Taking alleged gods for honor extends the surah's critique of imagined supports that fail before God.
The worshipped beings will disown their worshippers, reinforcing the claimant's final abandonment of every support.
God's counting of the disbelievers gives a nearby accountability frame for the claimant's appointed end.
The righteous are gathered as a delegation to the Merciful, contrasting with the claimant's solitary arrival.
The criminals are driven thirsty to the Merciful, a related final-return scene of deprivation.
The claim that the Merciful has taken a child broadens the surah's rejection of presumptions built around offspring.
The Merciful's transcendence above taking a child sharply qualifies all assertions of lineage and offspring before Him.
Wealth and children are only the adornment of worldly life; lasting righteous deeds have the better final reward.
Each person's deeds are bound to him and will be produced as an opened record on the Day of Resurrection.
The individual is commanded to read his own record, closely matching the focus's personal accountability.
God records what people send ahead and what they leave behind, directly supporting the focus's divine taking and accounting.
God's record speaks truthfully against people on the Day of Judgment, paralleling the focus's answer to what the claimant says.
No utterance is made without a ready recorder, directly illuminating the focus's reckoning of speech.
Every deed is preserved in written records, supporting the focus's accounting of the claimant's words and possessions.
God informs people of what they did after having enumerated it while they forgot it.
The recipient of the record in his left hand enters judgment stripped of worldly security and hope.
God has enumerated everything in a record, providing a broad record-keeping parallel.
On that Day the course is driven to the Lord, directly paralleling the claimant's coming to God.
No soul can avail another soul on the Day when all command belongs to God, clarifying the claimant's aloneness.
Neither wealth nor children can avail disbelievers against God, directly negating the supports claimed in the context.
On the Day of Judgment neither wealth nor sons will benefit anyone, the closest explicit parallel to the claimant's boast.
Wealth and children must not distract from God's remembrance; those they distract are the losers.
At death, the delayed person regrets not having given and done good deeds, showing the final failure of worldly delay.
Wealth and children are a trial, not a secure possession, directly correcting the claimant's assumption.
Wealth and children can become a means of punishment rather than a sign of favor.
God's granting of abundant wealth to a hostile man closely parallels the focus's reversal of a boastful claimant's wealth.
The granting of sons present with him directly parallels the claimant's claim to children and their impermanence.
A person's wealth will not avail when he falls, a concise direct negation of reliance on possession.
Rivalry in accumulating more distracts people until they reach the graves, contrasting sharply with the focus's final return.
The hoarder who counts his wealth embodies the same false reliance on possession answered in the focus.
He imagines wealth will make him immortal, a direct illusion overturned by the claimant's solitary coming to God.
Abu Lahab's wealth and gains do not avail him, directly paralleling the failure of claimed material security.
When the Trumpet is blown, family ties no longer function among people, strongly clarifying why one comes alone.
On the Day of Judgment no close friend asks after another, supporting the focus's lack of companionship.
People are shown one another, yet the sinner would ransom himself with his sons, directly linking judgment and failed offspring.
The sinner would sacrifice his wife and brother to escape punishment, showing the collapse of family support.
Even one's protecting clan cannot secure rescue on that Day.
On that Day a person flees from his brother, vividly extending the focus's solitary arrival.
A person flees from his mother and father, showing that kinship cannot accompany final accountability.
A person flees from his spouse and children, directly negating reliance on family accompaniment.
Neither parent nor child can avail the other before God, a family-specific parallel to solitary judgment.
